Abstract.

Let α=a/q+ϵ\alpha=a/q+\epsilon with (a,q)=1(a,q)=1, q⩽N1/2q\leqslant N^{1/2} and |ϵ|⩽1/(q​N1/2)|\epsilon|\leqslant 1/(qN^{1/2}), and let B:=max⁡(q,q​N​|ϵ|)B:=\max(q,qN|\epsilon|). We show that

|∑n<NΛ⁡(n)​e​(n​α)|⩽No⁡(1)​(NB1/2+N19/24).\Bigl|\sum_{n<N}\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha)\Bigr|\leqslant N^{o(1)}\Bigl(\frac{N}{B^{1/2}}+N^{19/24}\Bigr).

This improves on the classical bound of Vinogradov from 1937, which has N4/5N^{4/5} in place of N19/24N^{19/24}.

Key words and phrases: 
Exponential sums over primes, Dirichlet polynomials, large values estimates, zero density estimates
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
11L20 (Primary), 11L07, 11M06 (Secondary)

1. Introduction

Exponential sums over primes

SN​(α):=∑n<NΛ⁡(n)​e​(n​α)S_{N}(\alpha):=\sum_{n<N}\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha)

are a central object in additive prime number theory. Following Vinogradov’s resolution of the ternary Goldbach problem for all sufficiently large odd integers [9], pointwise bounds for SN​(α)S_{N}(\alpha) have been a key input to applications of the Hardy–Littlewood circle method involving primes. They also underpin results on the distribution of α​p\alpha p modulo one and on Diophantine approximation with primes.

By Dirichlet’s theorem on rational approximation, any α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} may be written as α=a/q+ϵ\alpha=a/q+\epsilon with (a,q)=1(a,q)=1, q⩽N1/2q\leqslant N^{1/2} and |ϵ|⩽1/(q​N1/2)|\epsilon|\leqslant 1/(qN^{1/2}), and the strength of the available bounds for SN​(α)S_{N}(\alpha) is governed by the quantity

B:=max⁡(q,q​N​|ϵ|)⩽N1/2.B:=\max(q,qN|\epsilon|)\leqslant N^{1/2}.

Vinogradov’s method, in the streamlined form given by Vaughan’s identity [8], shows that

(1.1) SN​(α)≪No⁡(1)​(NB1/2+N4/5)S_{N}(\alpha)\ll N^{o(1)}\Bigl(\frac{N}{B^{1/2}}+N^{4/5}\Bigr)

The exponent 4/54/5 has long stood as the limit of the classical methods for generic α\alpha. Our main result improves it.

Theorem 1.1.

Let N≥1N\geq 1. Let α=a/q+ϵ\alpha=a/q+\epsilon with (a,q)=1(a,q)=1, q⩽N1/2q\leqslant N^{1/2} and |ϵ|⩽1/(q​N1/2)|\epsilon|\leqslant 1/(qN^{1/2}). Let B:=max⁡(q,q​N​|ϵ|)B:=\max(q,qN|\epsilon|). Then we have

|∑n<NΛ⁡(n)​e​(n​α)|⩽No⁡(1)​(NB1/2+N19/24).\Big|\sum_{n<N}\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha)\Big|\leqslant N^{o(1)}\Bigl(\frac{N}{B^{1/2}}+N^{19/24}\Bigr).

Theorem 1.1 should be compared with (1.1): it replaces the term N4/5N^{4/5} with N19/24N^{19/24} (note that 4/5=19/24+1/1204/5=19/24+1/120). The most important range for our result is when q≈N1/2q\approx N^{1/2}, which happens for ‘generic’ α\alpha. For qq smaller than N1/2N^{1/2}, Kumchev [5] obtained a bound with B1/2​N11/20B^{1/2}N^{11/20} in place of N4/5N^{4/5}. This is stronger than the bound of Theorem 1.1 whenever B≤N1/2−δB\leq N^{1/2-\delta} with δ>1/60\delta>1/60 (the terms B1/2​N11/20B^{1/2}N^{11/20} and N19/24N^{19/24} cross at B=N29/60B=N^{29/60}), but such α\alpha form a set of measure shrinking to zero as N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. Moreover, there is a large literature obtaining bounds of the form

≪NB1/2\ll\frac{N}{B^{1/2}}

for B≤NδB\leq N^{\delta} with small δ>0\delta>0.

Morally one can think of the N/B1/2N/B^{1/2} term as coming from possible exceptional zeros with ℜ⁡(s)\Re(s) close to 1; this term can be improved for all qq outside of a thin exceptional set. Under GRH we have the stronger estimate

∑n<NΛ⁡(n)​e​(n​α)=μ⁡(q)ϕ⁡(q)​∑n<Ne⁡(n​ϵ)+O⁡(N1/2+o⁡(1)​B1/2),\sum_{n<N}\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha)=\frac{\mu(q)}{\phi(q)}\sum_{n<N}e(n\epsilon)+O(N^{1/2+o(1)}B^{1/2}),

which gives an O⁡(N3/4)O(N^{3/4}) error term in the case of q≈N1/2q\approx N^{1/2}.

Our proof combines the Heath-Brown identity with mean value theorems and fourth moment estimates for Dirichlet polynomials and LL-functions, together with recent large values estimates for Dirichlet polynomials in the qq-aspect [1], extending work of Guth and the first author [2]. As sketched in Section 2, inserting these large values estimates into the standard zero density framework already improves the exponent 4/54/5 to 67/8467/84; the stronger exponent 19/2419/24 of Theorem 1.1 comes from working with the Dirichlet polynomials directly, exploiting the fact that the critical factorizations behind the zero density argument cannot actually occur.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we outline the argument. In Section 3 we prove our main technical result, Proposition 3.11, which bounds the exponential sum over a dyadic range n∼xn\sim x when B∈[x4/9,x1/2]B\in[x^{4/9},x^{1/2}]. In Section 4 we deduce Theorem 1.1 from Proposition 3.11 via a dyadic decomposition, using an estimate of Kumchev [5] for the ranges where BB is small.

2. Outline

As a proof-of-concept, let us sketch how to obtain an improvement over Kumchev’s bound for a smoothed version of the sum in Theorem 1.1. Let ww be a smooth function, compactly supported in (1/2,5/2)(1/2,5/2). Splitting the sum into arithmetic progressions mod​q\mathrm{mod}\ q via Dirichlet characters and then using Mellin inversion gives

∑nw⁡(nx)​Λ​(n)​e​(n​α)\displaystyle\sum_{n}w\Bigl(\frac{n}{x}\Bigr)\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha) =1ϕ⁡(q)​∑χ⁡(mod​q)∑b⁡(mod​q)χ⁡(b)​e​(a​bq)​∑nΛ⁡(n)​χ¯​(n)​w​(nx)​e​(n​ϵ)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\phi(q)}\sum_{\chi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)}\sum_{b\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)}\chi(b)e\Bigl(\frac{ab}{q}\Bigr)\sum_{n}\Lambda(n)\overline{\chi}(n)w\Bigl(\frac{n}{x}\Bigr)e(n\epsilon)
=−∑χ⁡(mod​q)τ⁡(χ)​χ¯​(a)2​π​i​ϕ​(q)∫c−i​∞c+i​∞Wx,ϵ(s)L′L(s,χ¯)ds,\displaystyle=-\sum_{\chi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)}\frac{\tau(\chi)\overline{\chi}(a)}{2\pi i\phi(q)}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}W_{x,\epsilon}(s)\frac{L^{\prime}}{L}(s,\overline{\chi})ds,

where τ⁡(χ)\tau(\chi) is the Gauss sum, and Wx,ϵ​(s)W_{x,\epsilon}(s) is the Mellin transform of e⁡(n​ϵ)​w​(n/x)e(n\epsilon)w(n/x). Shifting contours (and ignoring the residual contour), we find

∑nw⁡(nx)​Λ​(n)​e​(n​α)\displaystyle\sum_{n}w\Bigl(\frac{n}{x}\Bigr)\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha) ≈Wx,ϵ​(1)ϕ⁡(q)+O⁡(∑χ⁡(mod​q)1q1/2​∑L⁡(ρ,χ¯)=0|Wx,ϵ​(ρ)|).\displaystyle\approx\frac{W_{x,\epsilon}(1)}{\phi(q)}+O\Bigl(\sum_{\chi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)}\frac{1}{q^{1/2}}\sum_{L(\rho,\overline{\chi})=0}|W_{x,\epsilon}(\rho)|\Bigr).

It turns out that Wx,ϵ​(ρ)W_{x,\epsilon}(\rho) is small unless |ℑ⁡ρ|≍T:=max⁡(1,x​|ϵ|)|\Im{\rho}|\asymp T:=\max(1,x|\epsilon|), in which case |Wx,ϵ​(ρ)|≈xℜ⁡(ρ)/T1/2|W_{x,\epsilon}(\rho)|\approx x^{\Re(\rho)}/T^{1/2}, while Wx,ϵ​(1)≪x/TW_{x,\epsilon}(1)\ll x/T. This gives

∑nw⁡(nx)​Λ​(n)​e​(n​α)⪅xq​T+supσxσ​∑χ⁡(mod​q)N⁡(σ,T,χ)(q​T)1/2.\displaystyle\sum_{n}w\Bigl(\frac{n}{x}\Bigr)\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha)\lessapprox\frac{x}{qT}+\sup_{\sigma}\frac{x^{\sigma}\sum_{\chi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)}N(\sigma,T,\chi)}{(qT)^{1/2}}.

Using the new zero density bound ∑χN⁡(σ,T,χ)≪(q​T)7​(1−σ)/3+o​(1)\sum_{\chi}N(\sigma,T,\chi)\ll(qT)^{7(1-\sigma)/3+o(1)} in the range σ≥5/7\sigma\geq 5/7, together with the classical Ingham-type zero density bound [6, Chapter 12], ∑χN⁡(σ,T,χ)≪(q​T)3​(1−σ)/(2−σ)+o⁡(1)\sum_{\chi}N(\sigma,T,\chi)\ll(qT)^{3(1-\sigma)/(2-\sigma)+o(1)}, in the range 1/2⩽σ⩽5/71/2\leqslant\sigma\leqslant 5/7 (the two bounds crossing at σ=5/7\sigma=5/7), would then give the bound

∑nw⁡(nx)​Λ​(n)​e​(n​α)⪅x(q​T)1/2+x1/2​q1/2​T1/2+x5/7​(q​T)1/6.\sum_{n}w\Bigl(\frac{n}{x}\Bigr)\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha)\lessapprox\frac{x}{(qT)^{1/2}}+x^{1/2}q^{1/2}T^{1/2}+x^{5/7}(qT)^{1/6}.

Since q​T≪x1/2qT\ll x^{1/2} this gives the bound x/(q​T)1/2+x67/84x/(qT)^{1/2}+x^{67/84}. The exponent 67/8467/84 gives a small improvement over the longstanding classical bound of 4/54/5.

It turns out that the critical length LL of Dirichlet polynomials behind the zero density estimates for ∑χN⁡(σ,T,χ)\sum_{\chi}N(\sigma,T,\chi) in the argument given above is

L=q7/18.L=q^{7/18}.

When q≈x1/2q\approx x^{1/2} (which is the critical case for the exponent 67/8467/84), it is impossible to have all Dirichlet polynomials having combined length xx but individual lengths LL. Therefore, by working with the Dirichlet polynomials directly we are able to do a little bit better, ultimately obtaining the bound x19/24x^{19/24}, as in Theorem 1.1.

3. Proof of Proposition 3.11

Lemma 3.1.

Let ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, and let ww be a smooth function supported on [1/2,5/2][1/2,5/2] satisfying ∥w(j)∥∞≪j1\|w^{(j)}\|_{\infty}\ll_{j}1 for all j∈ℤ≥0j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. Let

Wx,ϵ​(s):=∫0∞w⁡(ux)​e​(u​ϵ)​us−1​𝑑u.W_{x,\epsilon}(s):=\int_{0}^{\infty}w\Bigl(\frac{u}{x}\Bigr)e(u\epsilon)u^{s-1}du.

Then we have

  • •

    (Bound for large tt): For any integer j≥1j\geq 1

    Wx,ϵ(σ+it)≪j,σxσ(1+x​ϵ|t|)j.W_{x,\epsilon}(\sigma+it)\ll_{j,\sigma}x^{\sigma}\Bigl(\frac{1+x\epsilon}{|t|}\Bigr)^{j}.
  • •

    (Bound for small tt): If ϵ>0\epsilon>0 then for any integer j≥1j\geq 1

    Wx,ϵ(σ+it)≪j,σxσ(1+|t|x​ϵ)j.W_{x,\epsilon}(\sigma+it)\ll_{j,\sigma}x^{\sigma}\Bigl(\frac{1+|t|}{x\epsilon}\Bigr)^{j}.
  • •

    (Bound for tt not close to saddle point): If t⩽−10​π​x​ϵt\leqslant-10\pi x\epsilon or if t≥−π2​x​ϵt\geq-\frac{\pi}{2}x\epsilon then

    Wx,ϵ(σ+it)≪σxσ1+x​ϵ.W_{x,\epsilon}(\sigma+it)\ll_{\sigma}\frac{x^{\sigma}}{1+x\epsilon}.
  • •

    (Bound for saddle point): If −10​π​x​ϵ⩽t⩽−π2​x​ϵ-10\pi x\epsilon\leqslant t\leqslant-\frac{\pi}{2}x\epsilon then

    Wx,ϵ(σ+it)≪σxσ(1+x​ϵ)1/2.W_{x,\epsilon}(\sigma+it)\ll_{\sigma}\frac{x^{\sigma}}{(1+x\epsilon)^{1/2}}.
Proof.

This follows from standard estimates. First note by a change of variables and the support of ww, for s=σ+i​ts=\sigma+it

Wx,ϵ​(s)=xσ+i​t​∫1/25/2w⁡(u)​e​(u​x​ϵ)​us−1​𝑑u.W_{x,\epsilon}(s)=x^{\sigma+it}\int_{1/2}^{5/2}w(u)e(ux\epsilon)u^{s-1}du.

The first claim follows now from integrating by parts jj times (and recalling that w⁡(u)≪1w(u)\ll 1 is supported on u∈[1/2,5/2]u\in[1/2,5/2]) where we integrate the usu^{s} factors and differentiate w⁡(u)​u−1​e​(x​ϵ​u)w(u)u^{-1}e(x\epsilon u) factors. The second claim follows similarly from integrating the e⁡(u​x​ϵ)e(ux\epsilon) factors and differentiating the us−1​w​(u)u^{s-1}w(u) factors.

Combining the oscillatory factors, we see that

Wx,ϵ​(σ+i​t)=xσ+i​t​∫1/25/2w⁡(u)​uσ−1​e​(u​x​ϵ+t2​π​log⁡u)​𝑑u.W_{x,\epsilon}(\sigma+it)=x^{\sigma+it}\int_{1/2}^{5/2}w(u)u^{\sigma-1}e\Bigl(ux\epsilon+\frac{t}{2\pi}\log{u}\Bigr)du.

Let g⁡(u):=u​x​ϵ+t​(2​π)−1​log⁡ug(u):=ux\epsilon+t(2\pi)^{-1}\log{u}, so that g′​(u)=x​ϵ+t/(2​π​u)g^{\prime}(u)=x\epsilon+t/(2\pi u) is monotonic in uu. If t⩽−10​π​x​ϵt\leqslant-10\pi x\epsilon then for all u∈[1/2,5/2]u\in[1/2,5/2] we have

g′​(u)⩽x​ϵ+t5​π⩽−x​ϵ,g^{\prime}(u)\leqslant x\epsilon+\frac{t}{5\pi}\leqslant-x\epsilon,

while if t≥−π2​x​ϵt\geq-\frac{\pi}{2}x\epsilon then for all u∈[1/2,5/2]u\in[1/2,5/2] we have

g′​(u)≥x​ϵ+min⁡(t,0)π≥x​ϵ2.g^{\prime}(u)\geq x\epsilon+\frac{\min(t,0)}{\pi}\geq\frac{x\epsilon}{2}.

In either case the first derivative bound for oscillatory integrals (see [7, Lemma 4.3], for example), applied after integrating by parts to remove the smooth factor w⁡(u)​uσ−1w(u)u^{\sigma-1}, shows that the integral is ≪σ1/(xϵ)\ll_{\sigma}1/(x\epsilon). Since we also have the trivial bound ≪σ1\ll_{\sigma}1 for the integral, and min⁡(1,1/(x​ϵ))≪1/(1+x​ϵ)\min(1,1/(x\epsilon))\ll 1/(1+x\epsilon), this gives the third claim.

For the final claim, we see that for −10​π​x​ϵ⩽t⩽−π2​x​ϵ-10\pi x\epsilon\leqslant t\leqslant-\frac{\pi}{2}x\epsilon and u∈[1/2,5/2]u\in[1/2,5/2] we have

g′′​(u)=|t|2​π​u2≥x​ϵ25,g^{\prime\prime}(u)=\frac{|t|}{2\pi u^{2}}\geq\frac{x\epsilon}{25},

and so by the second derivative bound for oscillatory integrals (see [7, Lemma 4.5]) the integral is ≪σ(xϵ)−1/2\ll_{\sigma}(x\epsilon)^{-1/2}. Combining this with the trivial bound ≪σ1\ll_{\sigma}1 as before gives Wx,ϵ(σ+it)≪σxσ(1+xϵ)−1/2W_{x,\epsilon}(\sigma+it)\ll_{\sigma}x^{\sigma}(1+x\epsilon)^{-1/2}, as desired. ∎

Remark.

Lemma 3.1 is stated for ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0. If ϵ<0\epsilon<0 then, since ww is real-valued, we have Wx,ϵ​(σ+i​t)=Wx,|ϵ|​(σ−i​t)¯W_{x,\epsilon}(\sigma+it)=\overline{W_{x,|\epsilon|}(\sigma-it)}, and so the same bounds hold with ϵ\epsilon replaced by |ϵ||\epsilon| throughout and with the saddle point region reflected to π2​x​|ϵ|⩽t⩽10​π​x​|ϵ|\frac{\pi}{2}x|\epsilon|\leqslant t\leqslant 10\pi x|\epsilon|.

Let 0⩽η⩽1/1000\leqslant\eta\leqslant 1/100, let k≥5k\geq 5 and let a1,…,ak∈[0,1]a_{1},\dots,a_{k}\in[0,1] be such that ∑i=1kai=1\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}=1 and ai+aj≥2/9−ηa_{i}+a_{j}\geq 2/9-\eta for all i≠ji\neq j. Then at least one of the following holds:

Lemma 3.3 (Heath-Brown Identity).

Let x≥2x\geq 2, let x4/9⩽B⩽xx^{4/9}\leqslant B\leqslant x, let χ\chi be a Dirichlet character modulo qq, and let s∈ℂs\in\mathbb{C}. Then

Si,j​(s,χ)=∑n∈Ii,jai,j​(n)​χ​(n)​n−s,Ii,j⊆[Ni,j,210​Ni,j],S_{i,j}(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\in I_{i,j}}a_{i,j}(n)\chi(n)n^{-s},\qquad I_{i,j}\subseteq[N_{i,j},2^{10}N_{i,j}],

for some lengths Ni,j≥1N_{i,j}\geq 1 and coefficients ai,j​(n)a_{i,j}(n) which satisfy

  1. (i)

    ∏i=1kjNi,j≍x\prod_{i=1}^{k_{j}}N_{i,j}\asymp x for all jj.

  2. (ii)

    Ni1,j​Ni2,j≥2−20​B1/2N_{i_{1},j}N_{i_{2},j}\geq 2^{-20}B^{1/2} for all i1≠i2i_{1}\neq i_{2}.

  3. (iii)

    ai,j​(n)≪no⁡(1)a_{i,j}(n)\ll n^{o(1)} for all n≥1n\geq 1.

    If Ni,j>B1/2N_{i,j}>B^{1/2} we have Ii,j=[Ni,j,2​Ni,j]I_{i,j}=[N_{i,j},2N_{i,j}] and either ai,j​(n)=1a_{i,j}(n)=1 for all nn or ai,j​(n)=log⁡na_{i,j}(n)=\log{n} for all nn.

Proof.

The Heath-Brown identity with parameter K=5K=5 (see [3]) states that, for all n⩽2​xn\leqslant 2x,

Λ(n)=∑j=15(−1)j−1(5j)∑m1m2⋯m2​j=nmj+1,…,m2​j⩽(2​x)1/5μ(mj+1)⋯μ(m2​j)logm1.\Lambda(n)=\sum_{j=1}^{5}(-1)^{j-1}\binom{5}{j}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m_{1}m_{2}\cdots m_{2j}=n\\ m_{j+1},\dots,m_{2j}\leqslant(2x)^{1/5}\end{subarray}}\mu(m_{j+1})\cdots\mu(m_{2j})\log{m_{1}}.

Multiplying this by χ⁡(n)​n−s\chi(n)n^{-s}, summing over n∈[x,2​x]n\in[x,2x], and decomposing each of the (at most 1010) variables of summation into dyadic ranges, we may write the left hand side of the lemma as a linear combination of ≪(log⁡x)10\ll(\log{x})^{10} restrictions to n∈[x,2​x]n\in[x,2x] of products ∏i=1kSi​(s,χ)\prod_{i=1}^{k}S_{i}(s,\chi) with k⩽10k\leqslant 10 (the restriction must be retained, since the condition m1⋯m2​j∈[x,2x]m_{1}\cdots m_{2j}\in[x,2x] does not factor through the dyadic decomposition), where each SiS_{i} is a Dirichlet polynomial supported on a dyadic interval [Ni,2​Ni][N_{i},2N_{i}] with ∏i=1kNi≍x\prod_{i=1}^{k}N_{i}\asymp x, and the coefficients of each SiS_{i} are identically 11, identically log⁡n\log{n}, or given by the Möbius function, the latter occurring only for lengths Ni⩽(2​x)1/5N_{i}\leqslant(2x)^{1/5}. Since B≥x4/9B\geq x^{4/9} we have (2​x)1/5⩽x2/9⩽B1/2(2x)^{1/5}\leqslant x^{2/9}\leqslant B^{1/2} for xx sufficiently large, and so every factor of length greater than B1/2B^{1/2} has coefficients identically 11 or identically log⁡n\log{n}.

It remains to arrange the pairwise condition on the lengths; this concerns only the products, and leaves the restriction to n∈[x,2​x]n\in[x,2x] unchanged. Within each product ∏i=1kSi​(s,χ)\prod_{i=1}^{k}S_{i}(s,\chi), as long as there are two factors whose lengths satisfy Ni1​Ni2<2−20​B1/2N_{i_{1}}N_{i_{2}}<2^{-20}B^{1/2}, we replace them by their product, a single Dirichlet polynomial of length Ni1​Ni2N_{i_{1}}N_{i_{2}}. Since each product begins with at most 1010 factors and each merge reduces the number of factors by one, the process terminates after at most 99 steps. At termination every pairwise product Ni1​Ni2N_{i_{1}}N_{i_{2}} with i1≠i2i_{1}\neq i_{2} is at least 2−20​B1/22^{-20}B^{1/2}, while any merged polynomial is supported in [1,2−10​B1/2][1,2^{-10}B^{1/2}]. The coefficients of a merged polynomial are Dirichlet convolutions of at most 1010 of the original coefficient sequences, hence still of size ≪no⁡(1)\ll n^{o(1)}. Finally, a polynomial of length greater than B1/2B^{1/2} is never produced by a merge, and so is one of the original factors, with dyadic support and coefficients identically 11 or identically log⁡n\log{n}. ∎

Let x≥2x\geq 2, T≥1T\geq 1, q≥1q\geq 1 x4/9⩽B⩽xx^{4/9}\leqslant B\leqslant x satisfy B⪅q​TB\lessapprox qT. αi+αj≥29−ηfor all ​i≠j.\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j}\geq\frac{2}{9}-\eta\qquad\text{for all }i\neq j.

Lemma 3.10 (Removal of the cutoff).

Let x≥2x\geq 2, 1⩽T≪x1\leqslant T\ll x and q≥1q\geq 1. Let F⁡(s,χ)=∏i=1kSi​(s,χ)F(s,\chi)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}S_{i}(s,\chi) be one of the products Fj​(s,χ)F_{j}(s,\chi) appearing in Lemma 3.3, whose parameter BB satisfies B⪅q​TB\lessapprox qT, and let F♯F^{\sharp} denote its restriction to n∈[x,2​x]n\in[x,2x], as there. If k⩽4k\leqslant 4 then

∑χ⁡(mod​q)∫−TT|F♯​(i​t,χ)|​𝑑t⪅(q​T)​x1/2+x,\sum_{\chi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)}\int_{-T}^{T}|F^{\sharp}(it,\chi)|dt\lessapprox(qT)x^{1/2}+x,

while if k≥5k\geq 5 and q​T⪅x1/2qT\lessapprox x^{1/2} then

∑χ⁡(mod​q)∫−TT|F♯​(i​t,χ)|​𝑑t⪅x+(q​T)1/2​x19/24.\sum_{\chi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)}\int_{-T}^{T}|F^{\sharp}(it,\chi)|dt\lessapprox x+(qT)^{1/2}x^{19/24}.

Since F⁡(s,χ)F(s,\chi) is entire and |F⁡(s,χ)|≪xℜ⁡(σ)|F(s,\chi)|\ll x^{\Re(\sigma)}, Perron’s formula on the line ℜ⁡(w)=0\Re(w)=0, truncated at height xx, gives

4. Proof of Theorem 1.1

In this section we deduce Theorem 1.1 from Proposition 3.11. We first record an estimate of Kumchev, which will handle the dyadic ranges where the Diophantine quantity BB is small.

Lemma 4.1 (Kumchev’s estimate).

Let x≥2x\geq 2 and let α=a/q+ϵ\alpha=a/q+\epsilon with (a,q)=1(a,q)=1, q⩽x1/2q\leqslant x^{1/2} and |ϵ|⩽1/(q​x1/2)|\epsilon|\leqslant 1/(qx^{1/2}), and set B:=max⁡(q,q​x​|ϵ|)B:=\max(q,qx|\epsilon|). Then we have

|∑n∼xΛ⁡(n)​e​(α​n)|⪅xB1/2+B1/2​x11/20.\Bigl|\sum_{n\sim x}\Lambda(n)e(\alpha n)\Bigr|\lessapprox\frac{x}{B^{1/2}}+B^{1/2}x^{11/20}.

In particular, if B⩽x9/20B\leqslant x^{9/20} then the right hand side is ⪅x/B1/2\lessapprox x/B^{1/2}.

Proof.

This follows from the case k=1k=1 of [5, Theorem 2]. The final claim follows on noting that B1/2​x11/20⩽x/B1/2B^{1/2}x^{11/20}\leqslant x/B^{1/2} precisely when B⩽x9/20B\leqslant x^{9/20}. ∎
